blocks.text: **Devmaxx topic:** CDNs. **Goal:** move bytes to the user, cut origin load, and cut cost.
A CDN is a network of **Points of Presence (PoPs)** distributed around the world. Each PoP holds cached copies of content and terminates TLS.

blocks.code:
User (Tokyo)
   │
   ▼  ~20 ms
[Tokyo PoP]  ──── cache miss ────▶  Origin (us-east-1)
   │                                  │
   │  cache hit (~1 ms)                │
   ▼                                  ▼
User gets content from the PoP      Origin serves everyone, pays egress

blocks.text: **What you get:**

items.text: **Lower latency** — the user fetches from a nearby PoP (10–30 ms) instead of a distant origin (150+ ms).
**Lower origin load** — most requests never reach the origin.
**Lower egress cost** — CDN egress is typically cheaper than origin egress (and origin egress is often free for cached content).
**Absorption of traffic spikes and attacks** — the edge absorbs volumetric floods.
**Edge compute** — run code near the user (request/response transforms, A/B tests, auth, personalization, geo-routing).

blocks.text: **What it costs:**

items.text: Cache management complexity (invalidation).
A cache in front of your app is a **consistency** decision (Ch. 06).
Vendor lock-in, per-request fees, egress charges.
**TLS termination at the edge** — the edge sees plaintext (relevant for PCI/healthcare).

blocks.text: A CDN decides whether to serve from cache using a **cache key**. By default it's the **full URL** (including the query string).
**The classic mistake:** `GET /api/products?page=2` and `?page=3` are different cache keys → the cache fills with near-duplicate entries → hit rate collapses.
**Fixes:**

items.text: **Ignore query parameters that don't affect the response** — configure a cache key that includes

blocks.text: only the parameters that matter (`?id=` yes, `?utm_source=` no).

items.text: **Normalize the URL** — strip tracking parameters, sort remaining query params, lowercase the

blocks.text: host, normalize the path.

items.text: **Vary on the right headers** — but be careful: `Vary: Accept-Encoding` is standard; `Vary:

blocks.text: User-Agent` or `Vary: Cookie` fragments the cache dramatically (each cookie value = a new cache entry).

**Rule: never `Vary` on `Cookie` for shared caches.** One cookie per user × millions of users = a cache with a 0% hit rate and full origin cost. Use `Cache-Control: private` for personalized content, or do personalization at the edge *after* the cache lookup.

rows: Shared caches may reuse for 1 day (browsers ignore it)
May be stored, but must be revalidated before use
Only the browser may store it
Will never change (use with hashed URLs)
Once stale, must revalidate — don't serve stale
Serve stale for up to 10 min while refreshing in the background
Serve stale if the origin errors

blocks.text: `s-maxage` vs `max-age`
`max-age` applies to **both** browser and CDN. `s-maxage` applies **only** to shared caches and overrides `max-age` for them. This is how you set a short browser TTL and a long CDN TTL:
→ browser revalidates every minute; the CDN serves it for a day.
Freshness computation

blocks.code:
current_age = max(age_value, now - request_time)
freshness_lifetime = s-maxage ?? max-age
response_is_fresh = (freshness_lifetime > current_age)

blocks.text: Plus `Expires` (HTTP/1.0) as a fallback. Understand this and cache debugging becomes easy.
Three main strategies:
4.1 Time-based (TTL)
The simplest and most reliable. Set a TTL matching how stale the content can be.

items.text: **Pros:** no coordination, no purge API cost, no purge latency.
**Cons:** staleness up to the TTL.

blocks.text: 4.2 Content hashing (the best practice)
Filename or URL includes a hash of the content:

items.text: New content → new URL → the CDN fetches it fresh. **No purge needed.**
Old URLs stay cached but are no longer requested.
**Cons:** you need a build step that hashes, and HTML referencing assets must be updated (or use

blocks.text: a manifest).
4.3 Purge / purge-by-tag
Call the CDN's API to invalidate a URL, a prefix, or a tag.

items.text: **Pros:** instant invalidation.
**Cons:** costs money (often per purge request), may take seconds to minutes to propagate

blocks.text: globally, and isn't atomic — some PoPs purge before others. **A purge is a race.**
**Cache tags**: you assign a tag (`tag=product-123`) to responses, then purge by tag. Much better than purging millions of URLs.
4.4 Surrogate keys / stale-while-revalidate
`Cache-Tag` / `Surrogate-Key` headers let you invalidate groups of objects without a purge storm.
**Design rule:** use hashing for versioned assets, TTL for everything else, and purge only for exceptional cases (a legal takedown, a leaked document).
The classic CDN use case. Details that matter:

items.text: **Compression**: Brotli (better than gzip) — but compress once at build time and serve the

blocks.text: pre-compressed file (`Content-Encoding: br`). Compressing per request at the edge burns CPU.

items.text: **Image formats**: AVIF (best), WebP, JPEG, PNG. Serve modern formats with content negotiation

blocks.text: (`Accept` header) and fall back for old clients.

items.text: **Responsive images**: `<picture>` + `srcset`/`sizes` — or use an image CDN (Cloudinary,

blocks.text: imgix) that resizes on the fly (at the edge, cached).

items.text: **Cache immutable hashed assets for 1 year**; HTML for 0–60 seconds with

blocks.text: `stale-while-revalidate`.

items.text: **Preload/prefetch** critical assets; avoid render-blocking resources.
**HTTP/2 and HTTP/3** — multiplexing reduces the number of round trips; HTTP/3 (QUIC) handles

blocks.text: packet loss better on mobile networks.
The modern "edge computing" model: run code in the CDN's runtime.
**Common edge patterns:**

items.text: **Geolocation** — route to the nearest region.
**A/B testing / feature flags** — no origin round trip.
**Request/response transforms** — rewrite URLs, inject headers.
**Auth at the edge** — verify a JWT or session before it reaches your origin.
**Personalization** — swap a cached page's header/footer per user.
**Bot management** — challenge suspicious traffic.
**Error handling** — serve a static error page if the origin is down (`stale-if-error`).
**Request collapsing** — collapse identical concurrent requests into one origin fetch.

blocks.text: **Edge compute limits** (verify per vendor): runtime duration (typically 10–50 ms), no TCP/UDP sockets, limited or no access to internal databases, limited API calls to other edge functions, and a smaller JS runtime (no full Node APIs).
**The personalization pattern (important):**

blocks.code:
Cache the *shared* page (HTML with placeholders)
At the edge: replace placeholders with user-specific data (from a small KV store or a token)

blocks.text: This gives personalized content at shared-cache hit rates — the "cached shell, dynamic hole" pattern. The dynamic data must be fetched by the edge worker (a fast KV lookup), not by the origin.
The most expensive CDN workload. Design points:

items.text: **Segmented video (HLS/DASH)**: break the video into 2–10s segments. The player fetches a

blocks.text: manifest and then segments independently.

items.text: **Chunked transfer**: segments are fetched in parallel → faster startup, easier bitrate

blocks.text: switching.

items.text: **Multiple bitrates (ABR)**: the player adapts quality to available bandwidth.
**Manifest caching**: short TTL (seconds) so the manifest reflects current encoding state.
**Segment caching**: long TTL (days) — content is immutable.
**Signed URLs**: restrict access, set an expiry. Use signed cookies for multi-file playback (a

blocks.text: signed URL per segment would need thousands of signatures).

items.text: **Token buckets + real-time metering** for concurrent-stream limits.
**DRM** (Widevine/FairPlay/PlayReady) for premium content.
**Live streaming**: low-latency (LL-HLS) vs. standard; origin must handle the ingest.

blocks.text: **Cost control:** aggressive segment caching, prefetch the next segment, avoid cache misses on the hot path (a cache miss on a video segment means the origin pays egress *and* the user sees a stall).
**Why multiple CDNs:**

items.text: **Resilience**: no single point of failure.
**Coverage**: some PoP networks are better in certain countries.
**Cost**: negotiate rates; failover on price.
**Dedicated vs. shared**: dedicated CDNs (Akamai, Fastly) offer better control and performance;

blocks.text: shared ones (Cloudflare, CloudFront) are cheaper and simpler.
**How to route:**

items.text: **DNS-based steering**: a DNS provider (Route 53, Cloudflare) returns different CDN endpoints per

blocks.text: region or based on health.

items.text: **Multi-CDN at the DNS layer**: e.g., `foo.example.com` → Cloudflare, `foo.bck.example.com` →

blocks.text: Akamai as a fallback.

items.text: **Anycast**: both CDNs announce the same IP; BGP picks one (traffic engineering control).
**Application-level**: a small "CDN router" service picks the CDN per request.

blocks.text: **Trade-off:** multi-CDN adds complexity (two purge APIs, two sets of rules, inconsistent caching). It pays off at large scale or when resilience is a hard requirement.
The CDN is your perimeter. Put controls here:

items.text: **DDoS protection** — volumetric floods are absorbed at the edge; your origin never sees them.
**WAF** — SQL injection, XSS, bot signatures.
**Rate limiting at the edge** (per IP, per ASN, per geo).
**Bot management** — challenge, block, or price bot traffic differently.
**IP allowlists / geo-blocking** — for internal or region-limited APIs.
**TLS termination** — free cert management, HTTP/3, and modern ciphers. But: the edge sees

blocks.text: plaintext (relevant for PCI scope) and you must configure origin→edge TLS properly.

items.text: **Origin shielding** — the edge fetches from a small set of shield servers, not the origin

blocks.text: directly. Protects the origin from a cache-miss storm and hides it.

**Origin shielding** is underused and valuable: without it, a viral post (cache miss on 50 PoPs at once) becomes 50 origin requests; with it, the PoPs fetch from 2 shield servers, which fetch once from the origin.
Real systems have **several caches**, and invalidating only one leaves stale data elsewhere.

blocks.code: Browser cache → CDN cache → Nginx cache → App cache (Redis) → DB

blocks.text: Invalidation must cascade. A common pattern: a **cache-version key**.

Invalidate by `INCR redis cache_version:product:123` → the old key is orphaned and expires naturally. This invalidates the app cache. To cascade to the CDN, include the version in the URL or use a surrogate key and purge.
**Push vs. pull invalidation:**

items.text: **Pull** (revalidate on TTL): simpler, no coordination; staleness ≤ TTL.
**Push** (publish invalidation on write): fresher; requires a reliable channel (pub/sub, CDC);

blocks.text: messages can be lost, so combine with a short TTL.

items.text: **Configure a CDN for a static site.** Serve hashed assets with `max-age=31536000, immutable` and HTML with `max-age=0, s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate`. Verify the cache headers with `curl -I` from two different "locations" (or a testing service) and confirm the age and `x-cache` values.

**Measure the cache-key explosion.** Put a page behind a CDN with `?utm_*` parameters and analytics cookies. Observe the hit rate collapse. Then configure the cache key to ignore those parameters and re-measure.

**Edge personalization.** Cache a shared HTML shell with `{{username}}` placeholders and a placeholder for a per-user banner; use an edge function (or a reverse proxy in front) to fill them from a KV lookup. Show that the origin is hit once per cache period, not once per user.
**Origin shielding simulation.** Put a CDN in front of an origin behind a cache. Purge the CDN and count the origin requests. Then put a shield in front of the origin and repeat.
**stale-if-error drill.** Point the origin at a broken address with `stale-if-error=86400` cached content and verify users still get served while the origin is down.

blocks.text: Good: "Static assets go to the CDN with hashed URLs and a 1-year immutable TTL; HTML is cached at the edge for 60 seconds with stale-while-revalidate. The cache key ignores tracking parameters. For personalized pages I'll cache the shared shell and fill the user-specific parts at the edge, so we keep a high hit rate without serving one user's data to another."

Better: "Media is the big cost — I'll use segmented HLS with long-lived segment caching, signed cookies for access control, and origin shielding so a viral asset doesn't turn into a stampede on the origin. And I'll set `stale-if-error` so an origin outage degrades to stale content instead of an outage."
Red flags: caching personalized HTML at the edge without noting the leak risk; no `Vary` /cache-key thinking; no purge strategy; ignoring origin shielding.

selfCheck.q: **What is a CDN PoP, and what are the three main benefits?**
selfCheck.a: A Point of Presence is a geographically distributed cache + TLS terminator. Benefits: lower latency for users, dramatically lower origin load (and egress cost), and absorption of traffic spikes and DDoS attacks.

selfCheck.q: **Why does `?utm_source=newsletter` in the URL destroy your CDN hit rate?**
selfCheck.a: Because the query string is part of the default cache key. Every campaign, referrer, and session creates a distinct cache entry — millions of near-identical objects, each fetched from the origin once. Hit rate collapses and origin cost explodes.

selfCheck.q: **What happens to your cache hit rate if you set `Vary: Cookie` on a shared cache?**
selfCheck.a: Catastrophically. Each distinct cookie value is a distinct cache key, so the cache holds one entry per user. With millions of users, the hit rate approaches zero and every request goes to the origin. Use `private` for personalized responses, or strip cookies at the edge and personalize after the cache lookup.
`max-age` applies to both the browser and shared caches; `s-maxage` applies **only** to shared caches (CDNs, proxies) and overrides `max-age` for them.

When the content changes slowly but you want the browser to revalidate often — e.g. HTML cached at the CDN for a day while the browser checks every minute. Also for assets where you want aggressive edge caching without users re-downloading.

selfCheck.q: **What is `stale-while-revalidate` and `stale-if-error`, and why do they matter?**
selfCheck.a: `stale-while-revalidate` serves a stale copy immediately while fetching a fresh one in the background (smoother UX, less origin load). `stale-if-error` serves stale content when the origin is failing (turns an outage into degraded service). Both matter because a cache miss during a spike or an origin outage is exactly when you can least afford the origin load.

selfCheck.q: **Why is content hashing better than purging for deploying assets?**
selfCheck.a: A hash change produces a brand-new URL, so the CDN fetches it fresh with no purge at all. The old URL stays cached but isn't requested. Purges are slow, cost money, and aren't atomic across PoPs; hashing sidesteps all of that.

selfCheck.q: **What are cache tags, and how do they beat purging millions of URLs?**
selfCheck.a: Tags let you group objects (all variants of a product) and invalidate the group in one API call, rather than enumerating and purging each URL. Purging a million URLs individually is slow, expensive, and error-prone.

selfCheck.q: **What is origin shielding and why does it matter?**
selfCheck.a: A tier of servers between the CDN and the origin that the PoPs fetch from. Without it, a cache-miss storm (a viral asset, a purge) sends thousands of concurrent requests straight at the origin. With it, the PoPs fetch from a couple of shields, which fetch once and serve the PoPs.

selfCheck.q: **How do you invalidate a cache in a multi-layer stack (browser → CDN → app → DB)?**
selfCheck.a: Include a cache-version in the key (e.g. `product:123:v7`) and bump the version on write, so the app cache is invalidated by orphaning the old key. For the CDN, use surrogate keys / cache tags and purge the tag, or include the version in the URL. The browser cache is handled by short `max-age` + `must-revalidate`, or by a versioned URL.

selfCheck.q: **What is the "cached shell, dynamic hole" pattern?**
selfCheck.a: Cache the page shell (which is 95% the same for everyone) and fill in the user-specific fragments at the edge from a fast KV lookup. You get personalized content at shared-cache hit rates, instead of making every request dynamic.

selfCheck.q: **Why does the edge seeing plaintext matter for compliance?**
selfCheck.a: Because the CDN terminates TLS, it decrypts the traffic and sees plaintext. For PCI-DSS, HIPAA, or anything with that requirement, the edge must be in scope (or you use end-to-end TLS to the origin, which some CDNs support).

selfCheck.q: **How do you protect a paid video stream from sharing?**
selfCheck.a: **Signed URLs/cookies with a short expiry**, bound to the client session/IP where possible; a **concurrency limit** (e.g. max 2 simultaneous streams per account); **DRM** for premium content; and monitoring for suspicious concurrency patterns.

selfCheck.q: **What does `stale-while-revalidate` buy you in the context of a 10x traffic spike?**
selfCheck.a: It removes the origin from the hot path entirely for the duration of the staleness window. A 10x spike hits the cache, gets served instantly, and the origin only handles the background revalidations — instead of the origin absorbing 10x and collapsing.

When you need resilience against a single CDN provider failing or being degraded, when you need better coverage in specific regions, or at a scale where you can negotiate meaningfully better rates. Not worth it for a small site: two purge APIs, two rule sets, inconsistent caching, and more to debug.
